options: Avocado rancher with a hobby shop
fact: Self-taught woodworker Sam Maloof, the first craftsman to win a MacArthur 'genius' grant, kept adding rooms, shops and studio included, until his 6-room house had 16 more. Then a new freeway was routed right through it, so in 2000 the whole house was moved about 3 miles.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Shopkeepers who also run the hotel
fact: As St. Elmo's mines died, the Stark family bought up the empty buildings to save them, a big reason this ghost town still stands. Annabelle, the last Stark, kept this place going as a 16-room boarding house, store, post office and telegraph desk into the 1950s.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Artist J. André Smith founded this experimental art colony in 1937 with money from philanthropist Mary Curtis Bok, and painters like Milton Avery came to work here. He wrapped it in Maya-inspired ornament, and it's now a National Historic Landmark and one of the Southeast's rare 'Mayan Revival' buildings.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Citrus grower with a packing shed
fact: One of the earliest prefab houses in the U.S., it arrived by steamship and mule cart in 1873, with its frame on the outside and the finish inside, hence the nickname 'Inside-Outside House'. Retired sea captain Pierce ran a cabinet shop downstairs, lived upstairs, and later became a bank president.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Banker Samuel Nickerson spent four years and $450,000 on this 'Marble Palace', reportedly Chicago's most expensive home when it was finished in 1883. Note the vault; the American College of Surgeons later took it over, and today it's the Driehaus Museum.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Charles Reynolds bought this plaza store-and-home in 1903 and remodeled it on borrowed money, including a mortgage from the parish priest. In 1913 the priest foreclosed, moved in, taught catechism in the store, and later left the whole place to his housekeeper.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Railroad lawyer with a big library
fact: Jasper Cropsey trained as an architect before going all-in on blazing autumn landscapes, and he even designed stations for New York's elevated railways. This was the Hudson River School painter's last home and studio.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: John Carter learned printing as an apprentice to Benjamin Franklin, then ran the Providence Gazette 'at the sign of Shakespeare's Head' and the post office from this house. His reporting on the Gaspee Affair got him arrested for libel.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Painter Sydney Burleigh built this studio building in 1885, and artists still work in it. H. P. Lovecraft made it the home of the young sculptor in 'The Call of Cthulhu'; when an editor who'd once lived there jokingly vowed to send a ghost at 3 a.m., Lovecraft wrote a poem at 3 a.m. that night.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: In 1882 investors from Dundee, Scotland bought this Texas ranch for $1.25 million and ran it for seven decades. Their guest house was nicknamed the 'Scotsman's Dive', and by about 1925 it held the offices of the ranch manager and bookkeeper.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Retired general with a war museum
fact: Cattle-ranch heiress Electra Waggoner met her husband while traveling in the Himalayas, and this mansion was built for the couple in 1903-04. A Texas town was named after her; the Whartons sold the house in 1911 to another cattle baron.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Henry Field owned a brickyard, and his maker's mark, cut into the brick molds, still shows up reversed on the paving bricks out front. In 1919 his company's president, Andrés Pacheco, took over the property, and Pacheco daughters still lived upstairs when HABS came.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Ferdinand Lindheimer fled Germany after a failed 1833 uprising, was shipwrecked, and reached Texas the day after the battle of San Jacinto. The 'Father of Texas Botany' also edited the town's German-language newspaper, printed right here in his house.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Mogul with big family and staff
Bachelor mine owner, lives at club
fact: Alfred McCune built railroads, went into Peruvian mines with J.P. Morgan and Hearst, and in 1900 built this 21-room mansion with servants' stair and butler's pantry. His 1899 Senate run deadlocked the legislature so badly that Utah sent no senator to Washington at all.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Painter who ended up a grocer
fact: Harrison Crandall served as Grand Teton's official park photographer, selling prints and postcards of the peaks to visitors. He built this studio cabin in 1925-26, then tacked on a bedroom and a grocery store.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Chicago's park bosses ousted Jens Jensen in 1900 for refusing to go along with graft, and he came back to run the whole West Park system. The 'dean of the Prairie style' of landscape design used this kitchen as his drafting studio.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Modernist Paul Schweikher built this as his own home and studio from 1938, complete with a Zen garden and a solar dressing room. He went on to chair the Yale School of Architecture.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: A radical free-thinker, anti-slavery journal was printed here, and its voice helped keep Missouri's Germans with the Union. Then Carl Strehly went into wine: cellar, tavern, and an upstairs dance hall.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Fancy Victorian brackets outside, but inside it's the old three-room Pennsylvania German plan with separate doors for parlor and kitchen; a rear addition held a luncheonette and grocery until about 1950. In 1977 the Army Corps of Engineers demolished it for a reservoir project.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Swiss merchant Conrad Meuly hauled $1,600 of goods on the Texan Santa Fe Expedition, was taken prisoner, and lost it all. He started over as a Corpus Christi baker and grocer and built this house and store with concrete-brick walls.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Joseph Barton bet a railroad was coming, founded a town named after himself, and bought this house's plans for $45 from a magazine. The railroad never came through, and his showpiece, meat-and-milk cooler and all, ended up anchoring a town that faded away.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Artist Frederic Bartlett got this beachfront land as a wedding gift from his father-in-law and designed the whole estate himself with no architecture training. His widow Evelyn, ex-wife of Eli Lilly, kept wintering here until 1997; giving it away was the largest single private donation in Florida history.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Peter Britt hauled 300 pounds of camera gear down the Oregon Trail, until his own wagon train split over it, and reached the gold camp with five dollars. Note the skylit studio: his Crater Lake photos helped get it made a national park.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: William Jackson became the first keeper in 1869, with his wife Caroline as official assistant keeper: $1,000 a year between them. The lamp first burned lard, and every night someone had to haul the fuel up the tower.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Keeper Emmanuel Luick's wife Ella turned the official logbook into her personal diary. When he fell ill for three weeks in 1901, she nursed him by day and kept the light burning by night.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Jacob Wohlfarth, a former Menger Hotel chef, put up a wood-frame general store with a camp yard here in the 1880s and lived on site. It stood, much modified, until the early 1990s, and archaeologists later dug the lot hunting for a lost irrigation ditch.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Bill Menor homesteaded alone on the Snake River in 1892, ran a ferry, and tacked a store onto the east end of his cabin. When his brother Holiday moved in across the river in 1905, the two didn't speak for two years, yet Bill made his whitewash from Holiday's lime pit.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Conrad Beissel's Ephrata Cloister (1732) ran on extreme self-denial: members slept on 15-inch wooden benches with wooden blocks for pillows and ate one small meal a day. They also rose at midnight for a two-hour watch; this is the Saron, the sisters' house.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: At Watervliet, the first Shaker community, brothers and sisters got their own halves and staircases and sat on opposite sides of the shared meeting room. These celibate believers were also the first to sell seeds in little paper envelopes.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: This stone courthouse, finished in 1815, later served as the county jail. Before the town had a bell, the sheriff climbed the cupola and blew a huge tin horn to call court.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: This gold-camp jail was accepted on April 1, 1870. After the town's first schoolhouse burned in the 1880s, the front room served as the school for a while.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: San Quentin's Dungeon, built 1854, packed 14 tiny cells off one corridor. HABS says it may be the oldest surviving building ever built by the State of California.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Army laundresses were among the few women the Army officially recognized: they got housing and rations, and each soldier paid for his own washing. At Fort Union their 11 rooms sat right next to the guardhouse; in 1883 Congress cut the laundresses altogether.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Family of killers running an inn
fact: The Benders split their tiny Kansas inn and store with a canvas wagon cover, and daughter Kate handed out flyers billing herself as a healer and psychic who held séances. Travelers on that trail kept disappearing; in 1873, as a search closed in, the whole family fled and was never found.
credit: Wichita City Eagle, 1873 · via Wikimedia Commons (newspaper diagram)

options: Gambling boss with hidden back rooms
Con-man killer posing as a hotelier
fact: H. H. Holmes, a Chicago con man and murderer, added a 'hotel' floor for the 1893 World's Fair and refused to pay his architects and suppliers. The papers sold it as a 'Murder Castle' maze, but most of that was invented; its real hidden rooms hid furniture he'd bought on credit and never meant to pay for.
credit: New York World, 1895 · via Wikimedia Commons (newspaper diagram; sensational labels and shading removed)
